title: Define a network assessment
concept: Separate inventory, exposure, service configuration, segmentation and exploitation objectives. An asset list is not a statement that every test is permitted.
setup: Record exact owned lab targets, approved protocols, source zones, timing, credentials and stop conditions. Identify fragile devices and dependencies before active probes.
workflow: Begin with diagrams and existing inventory. Establish a baseline from one approved source, then select the smallest check answering a specific question. Keep discovery separate from vulnerability conclusions.
limits: A reachable host may be a shared gateway, proxy or reassigned address. Verify asset identity and scope before continuing. A successful scan does not establish authorization.
tools: Use ip, route inspection, Nmap explicit target/port selection and a flow worksheet. The supplied exercises stay on loopback or synthetic data.
retest: Report endpoint, transport, vantage point and time. Retest the same observation after the specific configuration repair.

title: Interfaces, routes and vantage points
concept: A connection depends on the selected interface, source address, route, listener and policy. Each source zone may see a different result.
setup: Record the intended source interface and destination. Distinguish host loopback, VM NAT, host-only adapters and bridged networks. Avoid publishing actual workstation addresses in reports.
workflow: Use local route and listener inspection before probing. Compare the application bind address with the destination clients use. A loopback-only service is usually inaccessible from a separate host.
limits: No route, no listener, filtering and application rejection are different failures. A failed ping does not prove a host is down.
tools: ip route, ip address and ss show local configuration; approved source-specific connections test the path.
retest: Repair the incorrect bind, route or policy at the responsible layer. Retest from both an allowed and denied source.

title: Host discovery and asset confidence
concept: Host discovery asks which addresses respond to chosen probes from a particular location. It does not prove that silent addresses are unused.
setup: Use an exact lab inventory or reviewed narrow address set. Understand whether the source is on the same link or across a router before interpreting ARP, neighbor discovery or ICMP results.
workflow: Start with passive inventory records when available. If active discovery is in scope, document the probe types and follow up only on approved assets. Correlate observations with authoritative inventory.
limits: A device can block discovery probes while serving an application. NAT can aggregate many devices behind one address. Neighbor tables may contain stale entries.
tools: Nmap discovery modes, ip neigh and managed switch inventory answer different questions. MAC-vendor information is a hint, not a verified device identity.
retest: Correct stale inventory and remove unintended exposures. Do not scan an entire network merely to fill missing documentation.

title: TCP and UDP scan interpretation
concept: A scan reports observations about selected transport ports. Open, closed, filtered and ambiguous states depend on probe method and responses.
setup: Select one configured service and a narrow port list. Know whether the method completes a connection and whether privileges are required. Set time and rate bounds appropriate to the lab.
workflow: Run the explicit localhost TCP-connect example in the workbook, then stop its listener and repeat. Correlate Nmap with ss and the application state.
limits: UDP silence can be ambiguous because services may ignore invalid requests and networks may drop replies. An open port is not by itself a vulnerability, and a port label is not confirmed software identity.
tools: Nmap -sT uses operating-system TCP connections; reason output and server logs help explain results. Version probes send additional application data.
retest: Close unused listeners or restrict their reachable sources. Retest the same protocol and port without assuming a TCP result describes UDP.

title: Capture placement and packet evidence
concept: A packet capture shows traffic visible at one observation point. It may not show both directions or traffic on other switch ports.
setup: Choose the correct interface and a narrow capture filter. Limit duration and packet count. Use only synthetic plaintext in a teaching capture and protect real captures as sensitive data.
workflow: Capture the local Ncat exchange, stop collection, then analyze the saved file. Locate the handshake, payload and closure. Compare packet timestamps with application activity.
limits: Retransmissions may indicate loss or capture artifacts; checksum offload can create misleading checksum warnings. Encrypted traffic usually exposes metadata but not application plaintext without appropriate keys.
tools: tcpdump captures and reads; Wireshark provides interactive analysis; TShark extracts selected fields. Capture and display filters use different languages.
retest: Preserve original capture evidence, record capture location and avoid presenting inferred application content as directly observed.

title: Segmentation and firewall policy testing
concept: Segmentation is an expected communication policy between zones and services. A VLAN name or subnet diagram alone does not prove enforcement.
setup: Create a matrix of source zone, destination asset, transport, port and expected reachability. Include management interfaces and permitted application paths.
workflow: Test each approved row from its stated vantage point and correlate with listener state and policy logs. Compare allowed and denied cases using the same destination service.
limits: Timeout is inconclusive without supporting evidence. A closed port cannot prove a firewall would block an active service. A successful TCP connection proves transport reachability, not successful application authorization.
tools: The offline flow evaluator teaches pass/fail/inconclusive reasoning using synthetic evidence; it does not change firewall rules or send packets.
retest: Repair overly broad policy, confirm required traffic still works, and preserve uncertainty where evidence cannot identify the failure layer.

title: DNS services and naming boundaries
concept: DNS resolution, authoritative data and recursive service are distinct roles. Naming correctness and service exposure require different checks.
setup: Identify the intended resolver, authoritative zone and whether recursion is expected for the source. Use fixture names and an owned DNS service for active testing.
workflow: Compare an expected answer with a deliberately absent fixture name. Record response code, queried server and TTL. Inspect split-horizon behavior only from approved zones.
limits: A cached answer can differ from current authoritative data. No answer can mean a valid empty response, NXDOMAIN, timeout or refusal; record which occurred.
tools: dig provides structured DNS observations. A broad zone transfer attempt is unnecessary for a basic resolution check and requires explicit test scope.
retest: Restrict unintended recursion or zone access, repair incorrect records and retest from relevant zones after accounting for caches.

title: TLS: transport protection and identity
concept: TLS can protect data in transit, but the client must validate the peer identity and certificate trust. Encryption alone does not authorize a service operation.
setup: Identify the expected DNS name, trust roots and whether mutual TLS is required. Preserve hostname verification instead of disabling it to make a check pass.
workflow: On a separately configured local TLS service, inspect the handshake and verify the name and trust chain. Then check application authorization as a separate test.
limits: An expired certificate and an unsupported protocol are different observations. SNI selects a virtual service but does not itself verify its identity.
tools: OpenSSL s_client and curl help inspect configured TLS; testssl.sh can perform a broader approved configuration review with additional probes. No TLS server is bundled in this new lab.
retest: Repair trust deployment, naming, expiry and obsolete configurations as appropriate. Retest using the same expected hostname and client trust policy.

title: SSH, SMB and SNMP service assessment
concept: Assess who can reach a management or file service, which identities can authenticate, and what authorized users can do. These are separate controls.
setup: Use supplied lab credentials and minimum needed privileges. Document account lockout behavior and permitted operations; do not guess passwords as a default assessment step.
workflow: Inspect configured algorithms and authentication policy for SSH, share permissions for SMB, and intended read scope and protection for SNMP. Compare one allowed resource with one denied resource.
limits: A banner version may be patched by a vendor without changing its advertised version. Successful authentication does not imply administrator rights or access to every share.
tools: OpenSSH clients, smbclient and SNMP utilities need separately configured services and credentials. The workbook provides decision guidance without inventing a working server.
retest: Remove obsolete services, restrict management sources and reduce permissions. Retest both transport exposure and application-level authorization.

title: Directory services and identity trust
concept: Directory-backed networks combine account identity, group membership, service permissions and trust relationships. Broad privileges can create indirect exposure.
setup: For an authorized directory lab, define read-only inventory rights, test accounts and data handling. Separate configuration review from credential attacks.
workflow: Map a small approved set of groups and privileged operations. Verify why a permission exists and whether inherited or nested membership changes effective access.
limits: A graph edge or group name is not sufficient evidence of an exploitable path. Preconditions, enforcement and actual privileges must be validated.
tools: Directory administration tools and approved read-only queries support review. Specialist relationship-mapping tools can collect sensitive data and need a defined collection scope.
retest: Reduce unnecessary privilege, protect service accounts and document legitimate dependencies. Retest effective permissions after changes.

title: Wireless and local-link trust
concept: Wireless enrollment, client isolation and management access are distinct security properties. Local-link protocols can influence neighbor and gateway decisions.
setup: Use an isolated radio lab with known devices and a recovery plan. Record authentication mode, guest policy and expected client-to-client reachability.
workflow: Review joining and ownership procedures, compare guest and management access, and inspect supplied captures. Keep active radio disruption and traffic interception outside routine configuration checks.
limits: A strong wireless password does not prove segmentation. Seeing a beacon or neighbor announcement does not establish that its claimed identity is trusted.
tools: Wireshark and vendor administration interfaces can support a controlled review. Monitor-mode capture depends on hardware, drivers and the intended channel.
retest: Repair weak onboarding and overly broad reachability, then retest guest isolation and legitimate access independently.

title: From service observation to verified vulnerability
concept: A service fingerprint or vulnerability-feed match is a candidate finding. Confirm the affected implementation, build, configuration and reachable feature.
setup: Record source evidence and vendor advisories. Prefer credentialed configuration or package evidence where approved, with least-privilege accounts.
workflow: Reproduce the smallest relevant condition on a resettable lab or verify the vulnerable configuration directly. Do not infer exploitability from a generic CVE label alone.
limits: Backported patches, disabled features and incorrect fingerprints can invalidate a match. A clean scanner result is limited by credential success and coverage.
tools: Nmap service observations and approved vulnerability scanners provide leads; vendor records and manual validation establish applicability. Review scripts before execution.
retest: Patch or mitigate the root cause, record residual exposure and confirm the service still performs its required function after repair.

title: Latency, throughput and availability
concept: Latency, loss and throughput measure different properties. A loopback benchmark mostly measures local software and host resources, not a physical network path.
setup: Use a brief bounded test with a known server and traffic budget. Avoid interpreting load-induced disruption as a useful default security test.
workflow: Run the three-second loopback iperf3 example, record duration and rate, and explain the measurement boundary. Repeat only when the changed condition warrants comparison.
limits: High latency can result from queueing, scheduling or a different route. Missing ICMP replies can reflect rate limiting rather than equivalent application loss.
tools: iperf3 measures throughput; ping or controlled application timings answer narrower reachability and latency questions. Capture evidence may help explain loss.
retest: Relate measurements to a requirement, isolate the cause and retest under comparable conditions without expanding load unnecessarily.

title: Network findings and remediation verification
concept: A useful network finding ties an unintended exposure or permission to a specific endpoint, source zone, observed behavior and business consequence.
setup: Use a worksheet with expected policy, test method, time, evidence and uncertainty. Redact actual system addresses and credentials in shared learning material.
workflow: Preserve original scan or capture evidence securely; summarize only needed details. Compare before and after from the same source and with the same selected service.
limits: An unreachable service after a fix may simply be stopped. Verify that legitimate clients still succeed before claiming correct segmentation.
tools: The supplied synthetic JSON matrix and assessment worksheet support repeatable review; they are not a substitute for live validation in an authorized environment.
retest: Record repaired, partly repaired and inconclusive outcomes distinctly. Include remaining assumptions and a concrete next verification step.
